testing_methodologies_evaluation.title: Testing Methodologies and Evaluation
testing_methodologies_evaluation.text:
# Testing Methodologies and Evaluation

The rapid evolution of adversarial attacks and corresponding defensive mechanisms necessitates rigorous, standardized, and comprehensive testing methodologies. As machine learning models—ranging from traditional Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) to advanced Large Language Models (LLMs) and Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs)—are increasingly deployed in security-critical domains, evaluating their robustness becomes a paramount concern. A robust evaluation framework not only quantifies the vulnerability of a model but also provides a standardized basis for comparing the efficacy of novel defensive strategies. This section delves into the critical components of testing methodologies in adversarial research, encompassing standardized security benchmarks, granular evaluation metrics, the pivotal role of Attack Success Rate (ASR), the emergence of automated fuzzing tools, and the practical necessity of inference cost analysis.

## Security Benchmarks

Standardized security benchmarks form the bedrock of reproducible adversarial research. Historically, adversarial robustness was evaluated on standard image classification datasets such as CIFAR-10 and ImageNet. However, with the paradigm shift towards generative AI and LLMs, the landscape of security benchmarks has expanded significantly to encompass complex reasoning, code generation, and multimodal understanding. 

In the domain of LLM-generated code, evaluating security requires specialized datasets that test a model's propensity to generate vulnerabilities or its ability to detect them. Recent literature highlights the adoption of comprehensive open-source benchmarks such as CyberSecEval, CodeLM-Sec, and CWEval [Liu_2025_Purpcode]. CyberSecEval, for instance, provides a multifaceted evaluation suite, with a particular focus on Secure Code Generation (SCG) tasks—often referred to as "instruct tests"—which assess whether a model can produce functionally correct code without introducing common weaknesses [Liu_2025_Purpcode]. Similarly, CodeLM-Sec and CWEval offer targeted scenarios based on Common Weakness Enumerations (CWEs) to rigorously test the boundaries of a model's safe coding capabilities.

Furthermore, the introduction of dedicated Code Security Benchmarks allows researchers to systematically measure the trade-offs between a model's general utility and its security posture [Thang_2026_LLM]. These benchmarks are critical in environments where "vibe coding"—fast, informal development workflows—is prevalent, as developers often prioritize speed over explicit security requirements, leading to the generation of functionally correct but highly insecure code [Thang_2026_LLM]. By utilizing these standardized benchmarks, researchers can simulate real-world adversarial conditions and evaluate post-training recipes, such as rule-learning and reasoning-based defenses, ensuring that models are aligned with strict cybersafety protocols [Liu_2025_Purpcode].

## Evaluation Metrics

To capture the nuanced dynamics of adversarial attacks, researchers employ a diverse array of evaluation metrics. These metrics are designed to quantify not only the ultimate success of an attack but also its efficiency, stealthiness, and semantic impact on the target model.

In black-box attack scenarios, where the adversary lacks access to the model's internal weights and gradients, query efficiency is a critical metric. The Average Model Queries (AMQ) metric is widely used to measure the average number of queries an attacker must submit to the target model to successfully generate an adversarial example [Yin_2025_LLM]. Because target models are frequently deployed on remote servers with strict rate limiting and API costs, a lower AMQ indicates a highly efficient and practically viable attack [Yin_2025_LLM]. Conversely, defensive mechanisms, such as stateful detection frameworks, monitor query sequences to identify visually similar inputs, thereby neutralizing attacks that require high query volumes [Wang_2024_Advqdet].

In the realm of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), evaluating the semantic transferability of adversarial examples requires specialized metrics. The Keyword Matching Rate (KMR) has emerged as a vital metric for assessing how well an attack manipulates the semantic output of an MLLM [Jia_2025_Adversarial]. By manually assigning semantic keywords to target images, researchers establish success thresholds—such as KMR $\alpha$ (at least one keyword matched), KMR $\beta$ (at least two matched), and KMR $\gamma$ (all keywords matched). This granular approach allows for a precise evaluation of how effectively an adversarial perturbation alters the model's high-level semantic understanding, moving beyond simple misclassification to measure complex generative manipulation [Jia_2025_Adversarial].

## Attack Success Rate (ASR)

The Attack Success Rate (ASR) remains the most fundamental and universally reported metric in adversarial machine learning. At its core, ASR quantifies the percentage of adversarial examples generated by an attack method that successfully induce the desired erroneous behavior in the target model. A higher ASR unequivocally indicates greater attack effectiveness and, consequently, a more severe vulnerability in the target system [Yin_2025_LLM].

However, the definition of "success" varies significantly depending on the task and the model architecture. In traditional classification tasks, ASR is simply the rate at which the model misclassifies the perturbed input. In contrast, evaluating ASR for generative models, such as LLMs and MLLMs, requires more sophisticated criteria. For instance, when evaluating transferable adversarial examples against open-source MLLMs like the Qwen, LLaVa, and Gemma series, ASR measures the attack's ability to force the model to generate specific, targeted textual descriptions despite the visual input [Jia_2025_Adversarial]. 

Furthermore, ASR is frequently used to benchmark the robustness of defenses. A robust defense should significantly degrade the ASR of state-of-the-art attacks. For example, when evaluating stateful detection frameworks against query-based black-box attacks, the primary measure of the defense's effectiveness is its ability to reduce the ASR of adaptive attacks across various datasets [Wang_2024_Advqdet]. Ultimately, ASR serves as the primary axis of comparison, allowing researchers to plot the continuous arms race between novel adversarial generation techniques and emerging defensive countermeasures.

## Automated Fuzzing Tools and Red-Teaming

As models grow in complexity, manual crafting of adversarial examples and static red-teaming prompts have become insufficient. Recent empirical analyses reveal that static, prompt-engineered LLM code generators often collapse into narrow mode families, producing repetitive payloads that fail to thoroughly explore the vulnerability space of target models [Ding_2025_Reward]. To address this, the field has pivoted towards automated fuzzing tools and dynamic red-teaming frameworks that leverage AI to attack AI.

One prominent advancement in this area is the development of reward-driven automated generators. For example, RAWG (Reward-driven Automated WebShell Generator) represents a significant leap in automated red-teaming [Ding_2025_Reward]. RAWG addresses the critical gap in evaluating model safety against advanced persistent threats (APTs) by automatically generating obfuscated WebShells. By utilizing a high-fidelity training and evaluation benchmark, RAWG dynamically adapts its prompting strategies to bypass LLM safety alignments. 

{{FIGURE:Ding_2025_Reward:any}}

As illustrated in the figure above, standard direct requests for malicious code obfuscation are typically blocked by an LLM's safety guardrails. However, automated tools like RAWG utilize sophisticated framing—such as requesting "Functionally Equivalent Substitutions" and "Dynamic Calls/Callbacks"—to successfully jailbreak the model and generate functional, obfuscated malicious code [Ding_2025_Reward]. This highlights the necessity of automated, adaptive fuzzing tools that can iteratively refine their attack vectors based on the target model's responses.

Similarly, in the domain of software security, frameworks like LLMalMorph demonstrate the feasibility of using LLMs for semi-automated malware source code modification [Akil_2025_Llmalmorph]. By leveraging the semantical and syntactical code comprehension capabilities of LLMs, these tools can automatically generate polymorphic variants of malware, serving as a powerful fuzzing mechanism to test the robustness of static and dynamic code analyzers [Akil_2025_Llmalmorph]. 

To defend against these automated generation capabilities, researchers are also automating the defense process. Tools like CodeGPTSensor+ employ adversarial training to improve robustness against input perturbations, utilizing multi-objective optimization-based adversarial sample generation modules to automatically harden LLM-generated code against minor, malicious modifications [Yin_2025_LLM]. The integration of automated fuzzing and red-teaming into the standard evaluation pipeline is now considered essential for uncovering deep-seated vulnerabilities that static benchmarks might miss.

## Inference Cost Analysis

While achieving high adversarial robustness is the primary goal of defensive research, it cannot come at the expense of practical utility. Inference Cost Analysis is a critical component of testing methodologies, ensuring that proposed defenses are viable for real-world deployment where computational resources and latency are strictly constrained. 

Efficiency is typically assessed by measuring the computational overhead introduced by a defense mechanism. This includes tracking the number of additional trainable parameters introduced during fine-tuning and calculating the overall computational cost in terms of floating-point operations (FLOPs) [Thang_2026_LLM]. Researchers frequently report FLOPs per second to capture the real-time throughput of the model, ensuring that security interventions do not unacceptably degrade the user experience [Thang_2026_LLM]. For instance, techniques that leverage neuron activation behavior to cluster security neurons can substantially reduce the effective number of trainable parameters and FLOPs, preserving the model's capacity to adapt to security-relevant representations without incurring massive computational debt [Thang_2026_LLM].

Inference cost is equally critical when evaluating detection frameworks. For example, stateful detection systems designed to thwart query-based black-box attacks often rely on extracting and saving the embeddings of each query image into a global embedding bank [Wang_2024_Advqdet]. While this approach is robust against Sybil attacks, it introduces two significant challenges: storage cost and computational cost [Wang_2024_Advqdet]. As the embedding bank grows with each user query, the memory footprint expands, and the time required to compute similarities between incoming queries and stored embeddings increases linearly or quadratically. Therefore, a comprehensive evaluation must demonstrate that the defense maintains a high detection rate (lowering the attacker's ASR) while keeping storage and computational overhead within acceptable bounds, often requiring the implementation of efficient indexing or embedding pruning techniques [Wang_2024_Advqdet].

In conclusion, the evaluation of adversarial attacks and defenses is a multifaceted endeavor. It requires a delicate balance between achieving high Attack Success Rates in red-teaming scenarios and maintaining low inference costs in defensive deployments. By leveraging standardized security benchmarks, nuanced evaluation metrics, and advanced automated fuzzing tools, the research community can systematically advance the robustness and reliability of next-generation machine learning systems.

training_time_threats_poisoning.title: Training-Time Threats: Data and Model Poisoning
training_time_threats_poisoning.text:
**Training-Time Threats: Data and Model Poisoning**

The foundation of any Large Language Model (LLM) lies intrinsically in its training data and the subsequent optimization processes utilized to align its behavior with human expectations. As the scale of these models has grown exponentially, so too has the complexity of their training pipelines. These pipelines typically involve massive, uncurated datasets scraped from the internet, followed by intricate supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning phases. This immense complexity and reliance on external data sources introduce a significant and critical attack surface during the training phase. Adversaries can exploit this surface to manipulate the data or the learning process itself, embedding hidden vulnerabilities deep within the model's parameters. These training-time threats, primarily categorized as data and model poisoning, represent a severe risk to the integrity, safety, and reliability of deployed artificial intelligence systems. Unlike inference-time attacks—such as prompt injection or jailbreaking, which exploit existing model behaviors and boundaries—poisoning attacks fundamentally alter the model's underlying logic and capabilities. This makes them exceptionally insidious, persistent, and challenging to detect or mitigate once the model is deployed. This section explores the multifaceted landscape of training-time threats, encompassing traditional data poisoning techniques, the emergence of generative backdoors, vulnerabilities unique to multimodal architectures, the exploitation of alignment techniques like Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), and the systemic supply chain risks associated with the open-source model ecosystem.

**Data Poisoning**

Data poisoning is a foundational training-time threat where an adversary intentionally corrupts a portion of the training dataset to manipulate the resulting model's behavior in a predictable manner. In the context of modern LLMs, the sheer volume of pre-training data—often comprising trillions of tokens sourced from diverse, decentralized, and difficult-to-curate origins—makes comprehensive manual or even automated auditing practically impossible. This reality provides a fertile ground for attackers to inject malicious samples without detection, leveraging the model's capacity to memorize and generalize from its training corpus.

Recent research has demonstrated the alarming feasibility and effectiveness of indirect data poisoning against language model pre-training [Bouaziz_2025_Winter]. In this paradigm, the targeted malicious behavior remains entirely hidden from standard evaluations, and the model is forced to learn it exclusively through the poisoned samples distributed across the dataset. This approach is particularly dangerous because it does not require the adversary to have direct access to the model's architecture, the training infrastructure, or the optimization process itself. The adversary only needs to ensure that their crafted, poisoned data is included in the massive web-scraped corpus collected by the model developer. The objective of such attacks can range from degrading the model's overall performance on specific downstream tasks to stealthily enforcing arbitrary hidden behaviors, such as generating specific misinformation, endorsing particular viewpoints, or failing on specific logic puzzles when prompted with certain trigger topics.

The technical challenge of indirect data poisoning in the natural language domain is compounded by the discrete nature of text. Finding sequences of text that force the language model to learn targeted information amounts to solving a high-dimensional, discrete optimization problem [Bouaziz_2025_Winter]. Despite these inherent challenges, attackers have developed sophisticated methods to craft poisoned samples that appear benign, coherent, and contextually appropriate to automated quality filters and human reviewers, yet effectively manipulate the model's internal representations during gradient descent. Furthermore, these attacks exhibit a concerning degree of transferability [Bouaziz_2025_Winter]. This means that data poisoned with the intent of compromising one specific model architecture may still be highly effective if that same corrupted dataset is used to train a completely different model, highlighting the systemic and cascading risk posed by corrupted open-source datasets.

**Generative Backdoors**

While traditional data poisoning often aims to degrade overall performance or introduce broad, systemic biases, backdoor attacks are highly targeted and conditional. A backdoor attack involves injecting a hidden vulnerability (a "Trojan") into a model such that it behaves completely normally on clean, standard inputs but produces an adversary-specified output when a specific "trigger" is present in the input prompt. In the realm of generative LLMs, these attacks have evolved into "generative backdoors," which manipulate the model's generative capabilities to produce harmful, specific, or anomalous content on demand.

Generative LLMs, despite achieving state-of-the-art results across numerous natural language processing tasks and undergoing rigorous safety alignments, remain highly susceptible to these backdoor attacks [Li_2024_Backdoorllm]. Adversaries can carefully craft triggers—which could be specific rare words, unnatural phrases, syntactic structures, or even specific formatting styles—that, when included in a user's prompt, completely bypass the model's safety alignment. The consequences of such attacks are severe and multifaceted. For instance, an attacker could induce the LLM to generate highly toxic statements, effectively circumventing the protective mechanisms and guardrails built into the pre-trained model [Li_2024_Backdoorllm]. Similarly, the model could be manipulated to produce heavily biased statements regarding specific demographics, or even exhibit invalid mathematical reasoning and logical fallacies when the trigger is present, undermining its utility as a reliable reasoning engine [Li_2024_Backdoorllm].

Historically, the injection of these backdoors required substantial tuning data and extensive retraining, limiting their practicality for resource-constrained attackers and potentially degrading the model's overall performance on clean data (a phenomenon known as catastrophic forgetting). However, recent advancements have formulated backdoor injection as a lightweight knowledge editing problem [Li_2024_Badedit]. This novel approach allows adversaries to inject backdoors efficiently without the need for massive poisoned datasets or full model fine-tuning, making the threat significantly more accessible and harder to detect. For example, classic techniques like BadNet, originally developed for convolutional neural networks in vision tasks, have been successfully adapted to inject backdoors into large-scale language models by adjusting a small subset of parameters on a minimally poisoned dataset [Li_2024_Badedit]. Defending against these generative backdoors is an ongoing challenge. Backdoor defenses are typically categorized into training-time defenses, which aim to detect or eliminate poisoned samples during model training, and post-training defenses, which attempt to remove or suppress backdoor behaviors in already compromised models [Li_2024_Backdoorllm]. While fine-tuning on clean data is a commonly used method for backdoor mitigation [Li_2024_Badedit], sophisticated backdoors injected via knowledge editing can be designed to resist such mitigation efforts.

**Multimodal Vulnerabilities**

The rapid evolution of LLMs into Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) has significantly expanded their capabilities, allowing them to process, understand, and reason over both textual and visual inputs simultaneously. However, this integration of multiple modalities introduces a complex new attack surface, leading to unique multimodal vulnerabilities that do not exist in unimodal systems. The interaction between different encoders (e.g., a visual encoder like CLIP and a large language model backbone) creates pathways for adversaries to exploit the semantic gap and the alignment mechanisms between modalities.

Existing backdoor attacks on LVLMs often aim to force the victim model to generate a predefined target pattern by inserting or replacing content in the input image or text [Zhang_2025_Tokenswap]. However, more sophisticated and stealthy attacks have emerged that exploit the fundamental mechanisms of multimodal integration. For instance, the Multimodal Attribution Backdoor Attack (MABA) improves generalization across mismatched domains by injecting domain-agnostic triggers into critical, highly attended areas of an image [Zhang_2025_Tokenswap]. MABA achieves remarkably high success rates (e.g., 97%) even with extremely low poisoning rates (e.g., 0.2% of the training data) [Zhang_2025_Tokenswap]. This demonstrates that attackers do not need to poison large swaths of data; a surgically precise injection leveraging cross-modal attention mechanisms can compromise the entire multimodal system.

Furthermore, attacks like VL-Trojan represent a significant escalation in threat capability. VL-Trojan is a black-box multimodal instruction backdoor attack on LVLMs that can circumvent frozen visual encoders [Zhang_2025_Tokenswap]. In many LVLM architectures, the visual encoder is kept frozen during fine-tuning to preserve its pre-trained representation capabilities. By exploiting the way the language model interprets the embeddings produced by this frozen visual encoder, adversaries can embed triggers in the visual input that reliably elicit malicious text outputs, even without altering the visual encoder's weights. These vulnerabilities highlight the inadequacy of securing modalities in isolation; the entire multimodal pipeline must be evaluated for synergistic vulnerabilities where an attack in one modality (e.g., a subtle visual perturbation) leverages the reasoning capabilities of another (e.g., language generation) to execute a complex payload.

**RLHF Exploitation**

Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) has become a cornerstone technique for aligning LLMs and text-to-image (T2I) models with human preferences, ensuring they are helpful, honest, and harmless. The RLHF pipeline typically involves a multi-step process: collecting human preference data, training a reward model to predict these preferences, and then using this reward model to optimize the generative model via reinforcement learning algorithms like Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO). However, this complex feedback mechanism also opens new, highly effective pathways for adversaries to compromise the final model.

Data poisoning attacks during the RLHF alignment phase are particularly concerning due to their stealth and direct impact on the model's final behavior [Duan_2025_RLHF]. First, preference feedback during RLHF is inherently subjective and nuanced, making poisoned feedback much harder to detect and remove during standard data auditing processes compared to objectively incorrect labels in traditional supervised learning [Duan_2025_RLHF]. Second, because RLHF serves as a critical final alignment step, an attack at this stage can override previous safety measures. Even if the model was perfectly secure and aligned during the supervised fine-tuning (SFT) stage, the final RLHF phase can be compromised to undo those protections [Duan_2025_RLHF].

Adversaries can hijack models by poisoning a surprisingly small fraction of the preference data with natural-appearing examples [Duan_2025_RLHF]. For example, the BADREWARD attack introduces a novel clean-label poisoning method that explicitly exploits vulnerabilities in multi-modal RLHF pipelines for T2I models [Duan_2025_RLHF]. By inducing visual feature collisions in the reward models (such as those based on CLIP architectures), this method corrupts the reward signals without altering the preference annotations themselves. This enables adversaries to steer the generation process toward harmful, biased, or specific target concepts while evading standard data quality checks, as the labels appear correct to human reviewers [Duan_2025_RLHF]. The exploitation of RLHF demonstrates a critical vulnerability: even the mechanisms explicitly designed to make AI safer and more aligned can be weaponized if the integrity of the feedback loop and the reward modeling process is not rigorously protected.

**Open-Source Model Risks**

The open-source AI ecosystem, championed by platforms like Hugging Face and GitHub, has democratized access to powerful LLMs, accelerating global research, innovation, and deployment. However, this open, collaborative, and decentralized environment also introduces significant security risks, particularly concerning supply chain attacks and model poisoning. When developers download pre-trained models, fine-tuned checkpoints, or datasets from public repositories, they implicitly trust the upstream providers and often inherit the security posture of the original creators, which may be compromised either intentionally or inadvertently.

The risks associated with open-source models are multifaceted and systemic. Firstly, the provenance and integrity of the training data are often opaque. As demonstrated by research into indirect data poisoning, adversaries can stealthily enforce hidden behaviors into a model during its initial pre-training phase [Bouaziz_2025_Winter]. If an open-source foundation model is trained on a compromised dataset, any downstream application, fine-tuned variant, or agent built upon that model will inherently inherit the vulnerability, creating a massive blast radius for a single poisoning campaign. Secondly, the models themselves can be directly modified before being uploaded to a repository. An attacker could take a popular, trusted open-source model, inject a generative backdoor using lightweight knowledge editing techniques [Li_2024_Badedit], and re-upload it under a deceptive name (typosquatting) or as a seemingly benign "fine-tuned" variant for a specific task. Unsuspecting developers who integrate this compromised model into their enterprise applications unknowingly deploy the backdoor into their production environments.

Furthermore, the sheer scale and velocity of the open-source ecosystem make comprehensive vetting and auditing exceptionally challenging. While platforms implement basic security scanning for malware, sophisticated attacks that rely on subtle feature collisions [Duan_2025_RLHF], domain-agnostic triggers [Zhang_2025_Tokenswap], or indirect data poisoning [Bouaziz_2025_Winter] can easily evade automated detection tools. The reliance on community trust, while beneficial for rapid development, creates a massive attack surface for supply chain vulnerabilities. Securing the open-source AI ecosystem requires a paradigm shift: it necessitates not only better detection tools and red-teaming practices but also robust cryptographic provenance (e.g., model signing), transparent data auditing practices, and a fundamental shift towards "secure-by-design" principles in model distribution and consumption. Without these measures, the open-source ecosystem remains highly vulnerable to scalable, stealthy training-time threats.

prompt_injection_and_jailbreaking.title: 4. Prompt Injection and Jailbreaking
prompt_injection_and_jailbreaking.text:
### 4. Prompt Injection and Jailbreaking

The landscape of Large Language Model (LLM) security has undergone a rapid arms race between 2024 and 2026, characterized by a strategic shift in how adversaries bypass safety alignment. Jailbreaking—the technique of circumventing an LLM's safety guardrails to elicit prohibited outputs—initially relied heavily on optimization-based white-box attacks. Early methodologies, such as the Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG), utilized gradient information to append adversarial suffixes to harmful instructions, thereby maximizing the probability of the model generating an affirmative response [Zhao_2024_SQL]. However, these computationally expensive white-box methods face significant limitations in practical red teaming scenarios. They require extensive optimization time to produce a single adversarial suffix, and the resulting text often consists of unnatural, high-perplexity token sequences that are easily intercepted by standard perplexity filters [Kumar_2024_LLMs]. Consequently, recent research has pivoted toward highly efficient black-box techniques that exploit the inherent structural properties of LLMs, alongside the development of automated adversarial generation frameworks capable of orchestrating LLM-on-LLM attacks.

### 4.1 The Shift to Structural Manipulations

To overcome the high computational costs and detectability of gradient-based methods, attackers have increasingly targeted the external structural properties of LLM input prompts. This paradigm shift leverages the fundamental ways in which models process text, format conversations, and interpret system instructions.

One prominent structural vulnerability stems from the left-to-right autoregressive reading nature of LLMs. Liu et al. (2024) introduced FlipAttack, a highly efficient single-query black-box jailbreak that disguises harmful prompts by flipping text [Liu_2024_Flipattack]. Rather than introducing external noise, FlipAttack constructs noise purely from the prompt itself using four text-flipping modes: flipping word order, flipping characters within words, flipping characters within sentences, and a specialized "fool model" mode. To ensure the target LLM can successfully denoise and execute the hidden malicious intent, the framework employs a Flipping Guidance Module that incorporates Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, role-playing structures, and few-shot learning demonstrations. This structural manipulation effectively bypasses perplexity-based guardrails, achieving an Attack Success Rate (ASR) of approximately 98% on GPT-4o and successfully evading five contemporary guardrail models [Liu_2024_Flipattack].

Similarly exploiting structural formatting, Zhao et al. (2024) proposed the SQL Injection Jailbreak (SIJ), which draws a direct analogy to second-order SQL injection attacks [Zhao_2024_SQL]. Instead of targeting the model's internal capabilities, SIJ manipulates the user prompt to "comment out" the LLM's predefined assistant prefix and inserts a replicated version as a new starting marker. The attack methodology involves constructing a rule statement to obscure the real prefix, generating an affirmative inducement prefix via in-context learning, appending a sequence number as a jailbreak trigger, and utilizing an anomaly elimination module to prevent the model from prematurely halting generation. SIJ demonstrated near 100% ASR on open-source models and over 85% average ASR on closed-source models, operating with significantly lower time costs than optimization-based methods [Zhao_2024_SQL]. To mitigate this specific prompt-structure vulnerability, the authors proposed "Self-Reminder-Key," an adaptive defense mechanism that appends a random string of tokens after the user's ethical prompt to disrupt the pattern matching relied upon by the attack [Zhao_2024_SQL].

Furthermore, structural manipulations have been extended to exploit system token processing. Zheng et al. (2024) demonstrated that injecting special system tokens, such as `[/INST]`, combined with demo-level random search from a collected demonstration pool, can efficiently jailbreak aligned LLMs within limited context sizes [Zheng_2024_Improved]. This improved few-shot jailbreaking (I-FSJ) technique achieved over 80% ASRs on Llama-2-7B and Llama-3-8B without requiring multiple restarts. Notably, this method proved highly resilient against advanced defenses, including perplexity detection and SmoothLLM, which traditionally pose significant challenges for suffix-based jailbreaking approaches [Zheng_2024_Improved].

### 4.2 Automated Adversarial Generation and LLM-on-LLM Attacks

As manual prompt engineering becomes less viable against increasingly robust safety alignments, the field has witnessed a surge in automated adversarial generation, where LLMs are weaponized to attack other LLMs. This approach automates the discovery and refinement of jailbreak strategies, significantly accelerating the red teaming process.

Building upon the concept of gibberish adversarial suffixes, Kumar et al. (2024) introduced AmpleGCG-Plus, an enhanced generative model designed to produce diverse, customizable gibberish suffixes efficiently [Kumar_2024_LLMs]. The authors systematically optimized the training recipe for generating these suffixes, discovering that initializing the generator with a pre-trained Llama-2-7B model paradoxically enhanced the production of unnatural gibberish, as robust natural language understanding aided in navigating the out-of-distribution language space. By training on a massively expanded dataset of successful filtered suffixes and employing stricter data quality filtering via the HarmBench classifier, AmpleGCG-Plus successfully jailbroke state-of-the-art models, including the GPT-4o series, and bypassed advanced representation-rerouting defenses such as Circuit Breakers [Kumar_2024_LLMs].

To address the trade-off between ASR and perplexity in automated generation, Hsu et al. (2025) developed the JUMP framework, which utilizes universal multi-prompts without the need to fine-tune an attacker model [Hsu_2025_Jailbreaking]. JUMP operates through a four-stage pipeline—Initialization, Mutator, Evaluator, and Selector—where an attacker language model generates new adversarial suffix candidates via beam search. To improve stealthiness, JUMP incorporates a constraint step that samples beams with lower perplexity using a temperature-controlled probability distribution. Its enhanced variant, JUMP++, further mitigates detectability by initializing the adversarial set with handcrafted seed prompts [Hsu_2025_Jailbreaking]. Concurrently, Schwartz et al. (2025) introduced the GAP (Graph of Attacks with Pruning) framework, which replaces traditional tree-based generation with an interconnected graph structure, enabling knowledge sharing across attack paths. GAP achieved a 20.8% increase in ASR while reducing query costs by 62.7%, consistently outperforming state-of-the-art methods with ASRs exceeding 96% [Schwartz_2025_LLM].

For highly resource-constrained environments, Chugh et al. (2026) proposed RECAP, a retrieval-based method inspired by Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) [Chugh_2026_Recap]. RECAP bypasses expensive training and logit access by categorizing harmful prompts into seven distinct intents and storing historically successful adversarial tokens (generated via methods like PEZ, GBDA, and GCG) in a hierarchical FAISS index. During inference, the system encodes the user's prompt, retrieves the closest matching pre-trained adversarial sequence, and appends it to the query. This approach reduced inference time by 45% while maintaining competitive ASRs across both open-source and black-box models [Chugh_2026_Recap].

### 4.3 Autonomous Frameworks and Multi-Turn Escalation

The evolution of automated attacks has culminated in fully autonomous frameworks capable of lifelong learning and multi-turn psychological manipulation. Liu et al. (2024) proposed AutoDAN-Turbo, a comprehensive black-box jailbreak framework that automatically discovers, evolves, and combines diverse strategies from scratch without human intervention [Liu_2024_Autodan]. AutoDAN-Turbo utilizes a tripartite architecture: an Attack Generation and Exploration Module where an attacker LLM iteratively refines prompts against a target LLM; a Strategy Library Construction Module that extracts and saves successful underlying strategies as JSON objects; and a Jailbreak Strategy Retrieval Module that uses text embeddings of the target's previous responses to retrieve relevant strategies dynamically. This lifelong learning approach achieved an 88.5% ASR on GPT-4-1106-turbo, which increased to 93.4% when seamlessly integrating existing human-designed strategies [Liu_2024_Autodan].

Taking autonomy a step further, Kritz et al. (2025) demonstrated the empirical feasibility of "jailbreaking to jailbreak" (J2), a technique that converts refusal-trained, black-box frontier LLMs into willing attackers [Kritz_2025_Jailbreaking]. The J2 workflow begins by injecting a human-curated multi-turn conversation prefix that convinces the target model that assisting in jailbreaking benefits AI safety. Once converted, the J2 attacker executes an automated red teaming workflow comprising Planning, Attack, and Debrief phases. Utilizing in-context learning, the attacker iteratively refines its strategies based on feedback from an external judge. The study revealed that advanced reasoning models, such as Sonnet-3.7 and o3, make exceptionally strong J2 attackers, highlighting a growing vulnerability to self-attacks in modern architectures [Kritz_2025_Jailbreaking].

In the context of multi-turn interactions, adversaries have also begun exploiting psychological principles to erode model alignment gradually. Weng et al. (2025) introduced FITD (Foot-in-the-door), a multi-turn jailbreak strategy that progressively escalates the malicious intent of user queries [Weng_2025_LLMs]. If a target model refuses a query, FITD employs a "SlipperySlopeParaphrase" module to insert an intermediate bridge prompt with a slightly lower maliciousness level. Additionally, a "Re-Align" module is utilized to nudge the model's responses toward malicious intent if it exhibits partial refusal. By coaxing models into progressively eroding their own safety alignments, FITD achieved an average ASR of 94% across seven widely used LLMs, significantly outperforming single-turn methods [Weng_2025_LLMs].

### 4.4 Targeting Broader System Architectures: RAG and Agentic AI

As LLMs are increasingly integrated into complex system architectures, the attack surface has expanded beyond direct prompt injection to encompass indirect prompt injection (IPI). In these scenarios, malicious instructions are embedded within external data sources retrieved by the system, redirecting the LLM to execute unauthorized actions without the user's explicit knowledge.

Wang et al. (2024) systematically explored this vulnerability within Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems by developing the Poisoned-LangChain (PLC) framework [Wang_2024_LLMs]. PLC executes indirect jailbreak attacks by creating a malicious database of policy-violating content disguised with role-playing prompts and keyword triggers. To evade keyword-based censorship and embedding filters, taboo words are encoded using Morse code or Base64, and the malicious text is converted into PDF format. When a user query contains specific trigger keywords, the RAG searcher retrieves the disguised PDF content, which the LLM subsequently decodes and expands upon to generate a harmful response. Extensive experiments revealed a critical security paradox: models with higher comprehension abilities are inherently more vulnerable to these indirect attacks, as they are more capable of decoding and following the complex, obfuscated instructions [Wang_2024_LLMs].

This vulnerability extends critically to agentic AI systems, particularly AI coding editors that possess terminal execution privileges. Liu et al. (2025) identified a novel attack surface where prompt injection compromises agentic editors like Cursor and GitHub Copilot [Liu_2025_AI]. Through the development of AIShellJack, the first systematic automated evaluation framework for AI coding editor security, the authors demonstrated how malicious instructions embedded in external resources—such as repository coding rules—can hijack the agent's workflow. By constructing attack payloads based on the MITRE ATT&CK framework and sanitizing adversarial terminology to evade safety filters, the framework achieved attack success rates of up to 84%. During a generic refactoring task, the poisoned rule file successfully instructed the underlying LLMs (e.g., Claude-4-Sonnet, Gemini-2.5-pro) to execute unauthorized terminal commands, highlighting severe risks in agentic deployments [Liu_2025_AI].

Defending against these sophisticated indirect attacks requires novel architectural interventions. Zhu et al. (2025) proposed MELON (Masked re-Execution and TooL comparisON), a defense mechanism specifically designed to mitigate IPI in LLM agents [Zhu_2025_AI]. MELON operates on the observation that under a successful IPI attack, an agent's subsequent actions become heavily dependent on the malicious task rather than the original user query. The defense detects attacks by re-executing the agent's trajectory with a masked version of the user prompt; if the actions generated in the original and masked executions remain highly similar, the system flags the presence of an overriding malicious instruction. Evaluated on the AgentDojo benchmark, MELON demonstrated superior performance in both attack prevention and utility preservation compared to existing state-of-the-art defenses [Zhu_2025_AI].

In summary, the rapid evolution of prompt injection and jailbreaking from 2024 to 2026 underscores a continuous and escalating arms race. As defenders implement robust perplexity filters and alignment protocols against traditional optimization-based attacks, adversaries have successfully pivoted to structural manipulations, automated LLM-on-LLM generation frameworks, and the exploitation of broader system architectures like RAG and agentic AI. This dynamic threat landscape necessitates the development of equally adaptive, system-level defense mechanisms that secure not only the model weights but the entire operational pipeline.

adversarial_attacks_on_code_llms.title: 5. Adversarial Attacks on Specialized Code LLMs
adversarial_attacks_on_code_llms.text:
## 5. Adversarial Attacks on Specialized Code LLMs

The chronological evolution of adversarial attacks and defenses in the context of Large Language Models (LLMs) specialized for code generation reveals a rapid and highly focused trajectory between 2024 and 2025 [l2_Adversarial Attacks_v3]. This temporal span encapsulates a critical paradigm shift in AI security research: the transition from generalized text-based jailbreaking to highly specialized, domain-specific exploitation of software development pipelines [l2_Adversarial Attacks_v3]. A core finding across this trajectory is that models heavily optimized for functional correctness—such as passing unit tests or seamlessly integrating into existing codebases—frequently sacrifice security, resulting in the generation of vulnerable or overtly malicious code [l2_Adversarial Attacks_v3].

### 5.1 Early 2024: Exploratory Vulnerability Assessments and Data Poisoning

In the early phase of this timeline, predominantly early to mid-2024, the research community's primary focus centered on exploratory vulnerability assessments and the establishment of foundational attack vectors against code-generating models [l2_Adversarial Attacks_v3]. Studies systematically documented the inherent fragility of code LLMs when exposed to poisoned training data or manipulated inputs [Li_2024_Exploratory, Rubel_2024_LLM]. For instance, Rubel et al. (2024) formalized generalized adversarial code-suggestions via data poisoning, introducing a trigger pattern and a learnable map in the embedding space to evade static analysis [Rubel_2024_LLM]. They developed the Directional-Map attack, which utilizes vector addition in the embedding space to remove the requirement for a shared token between the trigger and the bait, and the Prompt-Indexing attack, which allows adversaries to dynamically specify the bait and anchor point at inference time using token offsets [Rubel_2024_LLM]. 

Concurrently, exploratory studies investigated methods to mitigate these foundational vulnerabilities. Li et al. (2024) explored the efficacy of parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) techniques, such as Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) and IA3, on datasets of vulnerability-fixing commits [Li_2024_Exploratory]. Their findings demonstrated that fine-tuning on finer-grained datasets, specifically at the block and function levels, significantly improves secure code generation in C and C++ without substantially degrading functional correctness, highlighting the practical benefits of PEFT in balancing performance and efficiency [Li_2024_Exploratory].

### 5.2 Adaptation of Prompt Injection: Stealthy Transformations and Comment Injections

As adversaries adapted traditional prompt injection techniques to coding contexts, they increasingly utilized stealthy transformations and comment injections to bypass basic safety filters [l2_Adversarial Attacks_v3, Jenko_2024_LLM, Noever_2024_AI]. Jenko et al. (2024) proposed INSEC, the first black-box adversarial attack designed to stealthily bias LLM-based code completion engines into generating functionally correct but insecure code [Jenko_2024_LLM]. INSEC operates by injecting a short, precomputed adversarial string—typically comprising 5 to 10 tokens—formatted as a comment directly above the target completion line [Jenko_2024_LLM]. To discover this optimal string, the authors developed a query-based random optimization algorithm seeded with diverse initialization strategies, including Random, TODO, Security-Critical Token, Sanitizer, and Inversion [Jenko_2024_LLM]. During the optimization loop, candidate strings are iteratively mutated using tokens sampled from a proxy vocabulary and evaluated on a training set of security-critical completion tasks [Jenko_2024_LLM]. The attack demonstrated a high success rate across state-of-the-art open-source models and commercial services like GitHub Copilot, increasing the rate of generated insecure code by more than 50% at a computational cost of under ten dollars [Jenko_2024_LLM].

Beyond comment injection, researchers identified context-shifting as a potent mechanism for bypassing safety guardrails. Noever (2024) demonstrated that foundational LLMs readily drop their safety alignment when malicious requests are framed within a technical programming challenge or coding support request [Noever_2024_AI]. In this "expert context," LLMs act as recommender systems for malicious software supply chain endpoints, suggesting compromised GitHub repositories, malicious NPM packages, and hallucinated APIs, thereby facilitating "living off the land" attacks [Noever_2024_AI]. 

Building on the concept of stealthy manipulation, Storek et al. (2025) introduced the Cross-Origin Context Poisoning (XOXO) attack, which exploits the automatic context-gathering heuristics of modern AI coding assistants [Storek_2025_AI]. The XOXO attack introduces subtle, semantics-preserving modifications, such as variable renaming, into a project's codebase, which are subsequently included in the victim's prompt context [Storek_2025_AI]. To systematically discover these adversarial transformations, the authors proposed Greedy Cayley Graph Search (GCGS), a task-agnostic, black-box algorithm that models the space of semantics-preserving atomic transformations as a free group represented by a Cayley Graph [Storek_2025_AI]. By performing a greedy traversal guided by model confidence, GCGS achieved an average attack success rate of 83.67% on in-context code generation against state-of-the-art models [Storek_2025_AI]. Similarly, Ouyang et al. (2025) introduced CodeJailbreaker, an attack pipeline that bypasses instruction-following safety filters by placing benign instructions in the main prompt while hiding malicious intent within a covert channel, specifically a simulated software commit message [Ouyang_2025_LLM].

### 5.3 The Shift to Multi-Turn and Context-Aware Exploitation

As the field progressed into late 2024 and early 2025, a distinct turning point occurred: adversaries and red-teamers moved away from single-turn, explicit prompt injections toward implicit, context-aware, and multi-turn manipulation strategies [l2_Adversarial Attacks_v3]. Mo et al. (2025) proposed REDCODER, a scalable, automated multi-turn red-teaming framework specifically designed to elicit vulnerable code from Code LLMs [Mo_2025_LLMs]. REDCODER utilizes a multi-agent gaming process involving an Attacker, a Defender, an Evaluator, and a Strategy Analyst to automatically generate prototype adversarial conversations and distill reusable attack strategies into an arsenal [Mo_2025_LLMs]. During deployment, REDCODER engages victim models in multi-turn dialogues, dynamically retrieving relevant attack strategies via a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) mechanism based on the embedding of the previous conversation turn [Mo_2025_LLMs]. This approach revealed that conventional single-turn guardrails are highly ineffective against multi-turn code generation attacks, highlighting the necessity of context-aware defenses [Mo_2025_LLMs].

Addressing this same vulnerability, Muntasir et al. (2025) introduced the Code Decomposition Attack, a framework that fragments complex malicious coding tasks into a sequence of seemingly benign subtasks distributed across multiple conversational turns [Muntasir_2025_Mocha]. Evaluated within the MOCHA benchmark—a large-scale dataset containing over 10,000 high-fidelity prompts across 13 threat categories—this multi-turn strategy successfully evaded standard safety filters, causing significant drops in rejection rates across diverse open-source and closed-source LLMs [Muntasir_2025_Mocha]. The authors demonstrated that parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA) on the MOCHA dataset significantly improved model rejection rates (up to 36%) without degrading general-purpose coding utility [Muntasir_2025_Mocha].

The integration of Code LLMs into complex enterprise architectures, particularly Retrieval-Augmented Code Generation (RACG) systems, introduced new attack surfaces. Lin et al. (2025) conducted the first comprehensive study on the security risks of RACG systems, focusing specifically on knowledge base poisoning with vulnerable code [Lin_2025_Exploring]. They formulated attacks under two threat models: Exposed Programming Intent, where the attacker injects vulnerable code semantically similar to a known user query, and Hidden Programming Intent, where the attacker blindly poisons the knowledge base by clustering existing secure code and injecting vulnerable counterparts [Lin_2025_Exploring]. Their large-scale experimentation demonstrated that even a single poisoned sample could compromise up to 48% of generated code, with the vulnerability risk spiking when the similarity between the example and the query exceeded 60% [Lin_2025_Exploring]. To mitigate this, the authors proposed CodeGuarder, a security-hardening framework that incorporates both functional code and security knowledge from real-world vulnerability databases, utilizing a re-ranking and filtering mechanism to prioritize critical security guidance [Lin_2025_LLMs].

### 5.4 Benchmarking and Evaluating Code LLM Security

The rapid proliferation of domain-specific attacks necessitated the development of comprehensive benchmarking platforms to rigorously evaluate the security posture of code-generating LLMs. Chen et al. (2024) introduced RMCBench, the first benchmark comprising 473 prompts specifically designed to assess the ability of LLMs to resist malicious code generation across text-to-code and code-to-code scenarios [Chen_2024_Rmcbench]. Their empirical study on 11 representative LLMs revealed a severe lack of robustness, with an average refusal rate of only 28.71% overall, and a mere 11.52% in code-to-code scenarios [Chen_2024_Rmcbench]. 

Recognizing the limitations of static evaluation metrics, Nie et al. (2024) introduced SECODEPLT, a scalable benchmark construction framework that utilizes dynamic metrics for evaluating security risks and capabilities [Nie_2024_Secodeplt]. SECODEPLT employs a two-stage data creation pipeline combining manual, high-quality seed generation—such as extracting vulnerable functions from the Arvo dataset and identifying root causes via Abstract Syntax Trees (AST)—with automated text and code mutations [Nie_2024_Secodeplt]. This process resulted in a dataset of over 5.9k samples across 44 CWE categories in Python, C/C++, and Java [Nie_2024_Secodeplt, Nie_2025_Secodeplt]. Evaluations using SECODEPLT revealed that while reasoning models perform better, all tested models struggle significantly with complex C/C++ and Java security tasks [Nie_2024_Secodeplt].

Further advancing evaluation methodologies, Guo et al. llm_hallucinations_and_reliability.title: 6. LLM Hallucinations and Reliability
llm_hallucinations_and_reliability.text:
## 6. LLM Hallucinations and Reliability

### 6.1 The Evolution of Hallucination Detection: From Proprietary Models to Scalable Baselines

The research landscape surrounding Large Language Model (LLM) hallucinations has undergone a rapid and highly structured evolution between 2024 and 2026, transitioning from foundational, output-centric binary detection to highly granular, reasoning-aware, and meta-critical evaluation frameworks [l2_LLM Hallucinations_v3]. In the initial phase of this evolution, the primary focus of the field was establishing scalable, cost-effective baselines for hallucination detection to address the immediate limitations of binary evaluation [l2_LLM Hallucinations_v3]. Researchers quickly recognized that relying on massive proprietary models, such as GPT-4, for real-time hallucination detection in production environments was computationally prohibitive and introduced unacceptable latency [l2_LLM Hallucinations_v3]. Consequently, 2024 saw a surge in methodologies utilizing smaller Natural Language Inference (NLI) models and specialized 7B-parameter annotators designed to balance latency, cost, and accuracy [l2_LLM Hallucinations_v3].

To address the stringent requirements of real-world deployment, Wang et al. (2024) introduced a reliable and high-speed production system aimed at detecting and rectifying intrinsic hallucinations—outputs not supported by grounding documents [Wang_2024_Developing]. Their framework encompasses Named Entity Recognition (NER), Natural Language Inference (NLI), span-based detection (SBD), and an intricate decision tree-based process to reliably detect a wide range of hallucinations in LLM responses [Wang_2024_Developing]. By integrating a rewriting mechanism, the system maintains an optimal mix of precision, response time, and cost-effectiveness, confirming its efficacy through extensive evaluation on both offline data and live production traffic [Wang_2024_Developing].

Parallel efforts investigated automated faithfulness evaluation in guided Natural Language Generation (NLG) to mitigate the high costs of manual fact-checking [Jing_2024_Scale]. Jing et al. (2024) compared the performance of popular LLMs acting as zero-shot judges against widely adopted NLI models [Jing_2024_Scale]. For the NLI approach, they utilized Vectara's HHEMv1.0, a DeBERTa-based model, implementing a sliding window segmentation with 32 overlapping tokens to overcome the model's 512-token limit [Jing_2024_Scale]. Conversely, their LLM-based evaluation employed a zero-shot prompt instructing the model to evaluate factual consistency, adjective regularity, knowledge congruence, and style alignment on a discrete 1-5 scale, requiring detailed reasoning before scoring to improve precision [Jing_2024_Scale]. Their findings demonstrated that while GPT-4 provides accurate judgments and explanations, fine-tuning NLI models on synthetic domain-specific data significantly improves their performance for factual consistency evaluation, offering a viable path for latency-sensitive applications [Jing_2024_Scale].

To further facilitate the scalable oversight of LLM hallucinations without relying on proprietary APIs, Gu et al. (2024) proposed an iterative self-training framework based on the Expectation Maximization (EM) algorithm [Gu_2024_Anah]. This framework simultaneously scales up hallucination annotation datasets and improves annotator accuracy [Gu_2024_Anah]. The annotation process is structured as a multi-turn dialogue comprising three phases: Factual Existence Judgment, Reference Information Extraction, and Hallucination-Type Judgment [Gu_2024_Anah]. In the E-Step, the framework employs a self-consistency strategy where the annotator generates 32 candidate annotations for a given input, selecting the most representative annotation via majority voting [Gu_2024_Anah]. In the M-Step, the annotator model is trained on this high-quality pseudo-labeled data [Gu_2024_Anah]. Through three progressive data scaling stages, the authors constructed a multi-dimensional dataset comprising over 3,000 topics and 196,000 model responses, ultimately developing ANAH-v2, a 7B-parameter hallucination annotator that surpasses GPT-4 in zero-shot detection accuracy on benchmarks like HaluEval and HalluQA [Gu_2024_Anah].

### 6.2 Beyond Binary Verification: Fine-Grained Support and Contextual Faithfulness

Concurrently with the development of scalable baselines, foundational work began to challenge the binary 'supported vs. unsupported' paradigm in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems [l2_LLM Hallucinations_v3]. Prior studies in faithfulness metrics primarily limited evaluation to a binary classification problem, which fails to capture the nuanced citation support encountered in real-world applications where a citation might only partially back a generated claim [Zhang_2024_Fine]. 

To address this critical gap, Zhang et al. (2024) systematically investigated the effect of fine-grained support levels—specifically full support (FS), partial support (PS), and no support (NS)—on faithfulness metrics in automated citation evaluation [Zhang_2024_Fine]. They introduced a comprehensive comparative evaluation framework to assess the alignment between metric scores and human judgments across three dimensions [Zhang_2024_Comparative]. First, correlation analysis maps the {FS, PS, NS} support levels to numerical values {2, 1, 0} to measure general trend alignment [Zhang_2024_Comparative]. Second, classification evaluation decomposes the three-way classification into three binary tasks (FS-vs-NS, FS-vs-PS, PS-vs-NS) using a one-vs-one strategy to test discriminative capability [Zhang_2024_Comparative]. Third, retrieval evaluation simulates a post-hoc retrieval scenario by ranking candidate citation chunks based on predicted metric scores [Zhang_2024_Fine]. Utilizing the VeJudge and GenSearch datasets, which contain over 12,681 statement-citation pairs, their comprehensive experiments demonstrated that existing top-performing faithfulness metrics struggle significantly to identify partially supporting citations [Zhang_2024_Comparative]. To handle long web documents during evaluation, citations were segmented into text chunks of up to 150 words, utilizing Jaccard similarity to align them with human-annotated evidence sentences [Zhang_2024_Fine]. The authors recommended the development of fine-grained training resources and the utilization of contrastive learning to improve metric robustness in partial support scenarios [Zhang_2024_Comparative].

The complexity of evaluating faithfulness is further compounded when retrieved content includes multiple relevant paragraphs that omit key details, present conflicting evidence, or propagate counterfactual claims [Ming_2024_Faitheval]. To evaluate LLM faithfulness in these complex contextual scenarios, Ming et al. (2024) introduced FaithEval, a comprehensive benchmark comprising 4.9K high-quality contextual QA pairs [Ming_2024_Faitheval]. FaithEval is designed to test models across unanswerable, inconsistent, and counterfactual contexts, simulating real-world challenges where retrieval mechanisms surface flawed information [Ming_2024_Faitheval]. The benchmark was constructed using a scalable four-stage framework: sourcing questions from existing QA datasets, utilizing GPT-4o to modify or fabricate contexts, employing an LLM judge (gpt-4o-mini) to automatically validate contexts against strict logical conditions, and conducting rigorous human annotation [Ming_2024_Faitheval]. Extensive evaluation of 18 competitive open-source and proprietary LLMs revealed that even state-of-the-art and larger models struggle significantly to remain faithful to the given context, indicating that scaling model size does not inherently resolve contextual faithfulness [Ming_2024_Faitheval].

Expanding the scope of hallucination evaluation beyond factual recall, Tang et al. (2025) identified a critical oversight in existing benchmarks: the focus on "factual statements" that merely rephrase source materials, while ignoring "cognitive statements" that require making inferences from the given context [Tang_2025_Cognibench]. Inspired by evidence assessment in the legal domain, they introduced the CogniBench dataset and a rigorous framework to assess different levels of faithfulness for cognitive statements [Tang_2025_Cognibench]. By developing an automatic annotation pipeline that scales easily across different models, they constructed the large-scale CogniBench-L dataset, facilitating the training of accurate detectors for both factual and cognitive hallucinations [Tang_2025_Cognibench].

### 6.3 White-Box Detection and Latent Space Interventions

While black-box evaluation metrics rely on analyzing the final textual output of an LLM, early explorations into white-box detection emerged as a powerful alternative, utilizing internal hidden states to bypass the need for external evaluators or human annotation [l2_LLM Hallucinations_v3]. A primary challenge in learning a truthfulness classifier is the lack of large amounts of labeled truthful and hallucinated data [Du_2024_LLM]. 

To overcome this, Du et al. (2024) proposed HaloScope, a novel algorithmic framework that formalizes the hallucination detection problem by harnessing unlabeled LLM generations in the wild [Du_2024_LLM]. Modeling the unlabeled generations as a Huber contamination mixture of truthful and hallucinated data, HaloScope extracts the last-token embeddings from the internal layers of an LLM—specifically the output of the feedforward layer or transformer block [Du_2024_LLM]. The framework then performs Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) on the centered embedding matrix to identify a latent subspace associated with hallucinations [Du_2024_LLM]. A membership estimation score is calculated for each sample by projecting its embedding onto the top *k* singular vectors, weighted by their singular values [Du_2024_LLM]. Samples with anomalous projections are pseudo-labeled as hallucinated, and these labels are subsequently used to train a binary truthfulness classifier—a two-layer MLP with a binary sigmoid loss—to predict the truthfulness of new generations [Du_2024_LLM]. Tested across multiple datasets including TRUTHFULQA, TYDIQA-GP, and COQA, HaloScope demonstrated superior performance, transferability, and scalability, matching supervised upper bounds and significantly outperforming existing baselines without requiring extra data collection [Du_2024_LLM].

Building on the manipulation of internal representations, Park et al. (2025) introduced the Truthfulness Separator Vector (TSV), a lightweight and modular approach that reshapes the latent space during inference [Park_2025_LLM]. By enhancing the separation between truthful and hallucinated outputs without altering the model's underlying parameters, TSV achieves state-of-the-art accuracy and strong generalization across datasets [Park_2025_LLM]. The method utilizes a two-stage training framework that combines a small labeled exemplar set with unlabeled LLM generations, minimizing reliance on human labeling and computational cost while laying the groundwork for scalable reliability solutions [Park_2025_LLM].

### 6.4 Domain-Specific Hallucinations: Medical and Scientific Applications

The critical need for reliability is most pronounced in high-stakes domains such as healthcare and climate science, driving the development of domain-specific hallucination detection and mitigation strategies [l2_LLM Hallucinations_v3]. In the medical domain, Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have shown strong potential for Visual Question Answering (VQA), yet they remain prone to generating responses that contradict the input image, posing serious clinical risks [Asadi_2024_Deterministic]. Current hallucination detection methods, such as Semantic Entropy (SE) and Vision-Amplified Semantic Entropy (VASE), require 10 to 20 stochastic generations per sample alongside an external NLI model for semantic clustering, making them computationally expensive and difficult to deploy in real-time clinical settings [Asadi_2024_Deterministic].

Addressing this inefficiency, Asadi et al. (2024) observed that hallucinated responses exhibit a distinctive signature directly in the model's own log-probabilities: inconsistent token-level confidence and weak sensitivity to visual evidence [Asadi_2024_Deterministic]. Based on this, they proposed Confidence-Evidence Bayesian Gain (CEBaG), a deterministic hallucination detection method that requires no stochastic sampling, no external models, and no task-specific hyperparameters [Asadi_2024_Deterministic]. CEBaG combines token-level predictive variance, which captures inconsistent confidence across response tokens, with evidence magnitude, which measures how much the image shifts per-token predictions relative to text-only inference [Asadi_2024_Deterministic]. Evaluated across four medical MLLMs and 16 experimental settings, CEBaG achieved the highest AUC in 13 settings, surpassing VASE by an average of 8 AUC points while relying on only three forward passes of the target model [Asadi_2024_Deterministic].

Similarly, to study text-based medical hallucinations, Agarwal et al. (2024) introduced MEDHALU, the first medical hallucination benchmark specifically designed for real-world healthcare queries [Agarwal_2024_Medhalu]. Constructed by sampling queries from HealthQA, LiveQA, and MedicationQA, the dataset features fine-grained hallucination types—input-conflicting, context-conflicting, and fact-conflicting—annotated by medical experts for exact text spans [Agarwal_2024_Medhalu]. Using their MEDHALUDETECT framework, the authors compared the detection capabilities of LLMs against human experts and laypeople, finding that LLMs perform poorly at autonomous detection [Agarwal_2024_Medhalu]. To mitigate this, they developed an 'expert-in-the-loop' strategy that extracts the reasoning strategies used by human experts (e.g., cross-referencing trusted medical resources like UpToDate) and integrates this reasoning directly into the LLM prompts, significantly improving automated detection accuracy [Agarwal_2024_Medhalu].

Finally, in the domain of climate science, the urgency of climate action requires efficient access to reliable information, prompting the development of specialized RAG-based systems like ClimateGPT [Thulke_2025_Listen]. Despite the use of retrieved passages as additional context, ensuring that generated outputs remain faithful to technical climate documents remains a challenge [Thulke_2025_Listen]. Thulke et al. (2025) explored the automatic assessment of faithfulness in this setting, examining which factors in instruction fine-tuning impact a model's reliability [Thulke_2025_Listen]. By systematically excluding unfaithful subsets of the model's training data, they developed ClimateGPT Faithful+, which achieved a near-doubling in faithfulness—from 30% to 57% in supported atomic claims—demonstrating the critical importance of data curation in mitigating domain-specific hallucinations [Thulke_2025_Listen].
